1.note: Read as 2 Elul, since the next entries count days of the month (10 Elul, 14 Elul). It could also mean "Monday of Elul": 1 Elul 5538 was Monday 24 August 1778.

2.he: המיניסטרו הגדול של המלך על ענייני חוץ האיסטאדו
2.note: Italian words in Hebrew letters: ministro and stato ("state"); the "affairs outside" are foreign affairs. The minister is the Sardinian secretary of state for foreign affairs; he is not named.

3.note: Madame Adélaïde (1732–1800), daughter of Louis XV and aunt of Louis XVI. The Hebrew says "her granddaughter" (נכדתה), but Clotilde of France (1759–1802), sister of Louis XVI and wife since 1775 of Charles Emmanuel, Prince of Piedmont, was the daughter of Adélaïde's brother, the Dauphin Louis: her niece. The Ḥida evidently brought the letter from Paris.

4.note: Italian giardino, "garden"; probably the royal gardens behind the king's palace in Turin.

5.note: Read as Duca di Savoia (Duke of Savoy). The transcription has ובוך; on the scan the letter looks more like ד (ודוך, "and duke"). The King of Sardinia in 1778 was Victor Amadeus III.

6.he: וגם אשת המלך היא ממלכות צרפת
6.note: The queen, Maria Antonia Ferdinanda (1729–1785), was an infanta of Spain, of the Bourbon house that also ruled France; hence "of the royal house of France". The marriages listed are correct: Marie-Joséphine of Savoy married the Comte de Provence in 1771, Marie-Thérèse of Savoy the Comte d'Artois in 1773, and Clotilde of France the Prince of Piedmont in 1775.

7.he: סדר הבדלות מחתן שהייתי בביאה ראשונה
7.note: Printed מחתן; A. Freimann, Ma'agal Tov ha-Shalem (Berlin–Jerusalem 1921–34), p. 173, reads מזמן, "from the time when": so the 1885 printing has a misprint. His first visit to Turin was on his first mission, in the 1750s.

8.he: וחדשו כמה פרקים בהלכות קמיצה. ובורחים מהשליח שלא יהיו תחת אהל אחד
8.note: Two puns. "Taking a handful" (kemitzah) is the priest's handful of the meal offering; here it is closing the fist, stinginess. "Under one tent" is the law of a corpse's impurity, which passes to all under the same roof: they avoid the emissary as if he were a corpse.

9.note: A. Freimann, Ma'agal Tov ha-Shalem (Berlin–Jerusalem 1921–34), p. 174, reads שלש יהיו לכם (plural), "the three shall be yours": keep your three sequins. They answered by sending eight, with apologies.

10.note: "My dear one" (חמודי). Educated guess: Raphael was the bride's father or near kinsman, and this entry and the next are the Ḥida's betrothal. The gifts he gives on arrival suit a bride (a thimble in a silver case, scented water, silk handkerchiefs, a prayer book); a few days later he brings earrings from Livorno, Jacob Pereira sends two rings, and "the matter was made public"; a month later he marries Rachel in Pisa. That Raphael is the Ḥida's elder son, Raphael Isaiah, is less likely: the Ḥida calls his sons "my son", not "Signor". The blessing "who has kept us alive" is said on seeing a dear person after a long time.

11.note: Probably two Venetian double sequins (doppi zecchini), gold coins; the plural ending -os is Spanish.

12.note: Read as Spanish redomica, a diminutive of redoma, "flask, phial"; not certain.

13.note: Read as étui (French, a small case for needles and sewing things) and dedal (Spanish, "thimble"); עץ could also be Hebrew "wood": "a wooden thimble(-case)" with silver. Not certain.

14.note: Abbreviation not resolved; perhaps the initials of a name, or of a relative (אחי, "my brother"?).

15.note: A surname in Hebrew letters, read as Ferridas or Peridas; not identified. It is not the Pereira (פירירא) family named below.

16.note: Printed with an abbreviation mark: perhaps the surname Faro, or an abbreviation not resolved.

17.he: שנת גדו"ל יהי"ה כבו"ד הבי"ת הז"ה היא שנת תקל"ט
17.note: A chronogram: the marked words add up to the year. גדול 3+4+6+30 = 43; יהיה 10+5+10+5 = 30; כבוד 20+2+6+4 = 32; הבית 5+2+10+400 = 417; הזה 5+7+5 = 17; total 539, that is [5]539 (1778–79), as the text says. The verse goes on "the latter [glory of this house shall be greater] than the former" (Hag 2:9), a fitting wish for a second marriage: his first wife, Rachel, had died in 1773. A. Freimann, Ma'agal Tov ha-Shalem (Berlin–Jerusalem 1921–34), p. 177, dates the wedding ד' חשון, but "on Wednesday" fits 7 Ḥeshvan 5539 (28 October 1778), as the 1885 printing has it; 4 Ḥeshvan was a Sunday. Freimann's fuller text adds that the wedding was at the bride's home in Pisa, and that she was born on the second night of Passover 5510 (1750).

18.note: מב"ת is printed as an abbreviation and is not resolved; perhaps a family name or the initials of her father. Rachel was the Ḥida's second wife. If the guess in note 10 is right, she was of the family of Signor Raphael of Pisa.

19.note: צו"ע = צומח ועולה, "growing and rising", a usual blessing in marriage contracts ("במזל צומח ועולה"); A. Freimann, Ma'agal Tov ha-Shalem (Berlin–Jerusalem 1921–34), p. 177, writes it out in full in this entry.

20.note: Tripoli: probably Tripoli in Barbary (Libya), on the route between Livorno and Tunis, rather than Tripoli in Syria. "His arrival in peace" reads לש' as לשלום.

21.note: הג' = הגביר, "the gevir"; המ' is not certain, perhaps המרומם, "the exalted", or המעולה, "the excellent". Probably the same Signor Michael of paragraph 118.

22.he: נאסף הסי' אלאייולים הי"ו וטפס עמנו
22.note: Printed אלאייולים; A. Freimann, Ma'agal Tov ha-Shalem (Berlin–Jerusalem 1921–34), p. 179, reads אצאייולים; his note at p. 66 (n. 11) gives Acciaioli (ל and צ are easily confused in this type). וטפס is read as וטפם, "and their little ones".

23.note: Literally "on the shoulder" (cf. Num 7:9): probably carried in a chair. In part 4 he was carried in a sedan chair in Trieste.

24.he: וקודם ההפטרה יצאתי והלכתי למנחה יום ש"ק יו"ט ב'
24.note: The end of the sentence is short and may be read in more than one way: either he left before the haftarah and came back for the afternoon prayer, or he left and went home, and the last words date what follows. "The second festival day" is the second of the two closing festival days (21–22 Nisan) kept outside the Land of Israel.

25.note: Read as Italian spiaggia, "shore, open anchorage" (with a Spanish-style initial i-), that is, the ship lay at the Livorno roads until ten in the morning, and then he was taken to the lazaretto. It can also be read as España, "Spain" ("he had been in Spain until the 10th"), but then the dates of the entry do not agree, since he arrived on 18 Nisan and the boat overturned "at ten" (ביו"ד) on his way to the lazaretto.

26.note: Printed so, as two words, which gives no clear sense ("which was not like that of the captain"). Read as a misprint for לאנצה (Italian lancia, a ship's launch): "the launch of the captain".

27.note: The Blessing of the Sun is said once in 28 years, on a Wednesday in spring, when by the rabbinic reckoning the sun returns to its place at the Creation. 26 Nisan 5545 was indeed Wednesday 6 April 1785; 28 years earlier was 1757 (5517), on his first mission.
